chapters.title: Prologue: Don’t Be Afraid
chapters.summary: Carroll's charge sheet against his own profession: quantum mechanics is the most successful theory we have, yet physicists cannot say what it describes, and the field has treated that gap as unimportant. He sets out the book's three claims and its three-part route.

sections.title: Physicists don’t understand quantum mechanics
sections.summary: QM underlies chemistry, solid-state physics and every semiconductor, yet its basic question — what a wave function is and what happens in a measurement — is unanswered. Physicists use it as a reliable black box; foundations work earns no jobs, grants or prestige, and the measurement problem is taught as settled when it is not.

sections.title: Three messages and the road map
sections.summary: The book argues (1) QM can and should be understood, (2) the Everett / Many-Worlds formulation is the simplest and most promising way to do so, and (3) taking the wave function seriously reshapes how we approach quantum gravity, where spacetime itself may emerge from entanglement. Part One covers the basics, Part Two branching, Part Three spacetime.

chapters.title: Part One · 1. What’s Going On: Looking at the Quantum World
chapters.summary: Contrasts classical and quantum mechanics at the level of 'recipes'. Classical physics has a state (positions and momenta) and a deterministic law; quantum physics replaces the state with a wave function and adds special rules for measurement, which is where the trouble starts.

sections.title: The 'spooky' reputation and the book's plan
sections.summary: Einstein's 'spukhaft' label and the flood of 'quantum' self-help titles. Carroll's stance: prize clarity over mystery; present the experimental facts first, then the Many-Worlds sketch, then the history, out of chronological order.

sections.title: Classical mechanics: state and determinism
sections.summary: Newton's Principia reduces an object to position and velocity changing under forces. The state of a system is its positions and momenta (phase space); given forces, the future follows exactly — Laplace's demon. Two quiet moves: what exists (particles, fields) and what can be measured are the same thing.

sections.title: Measurement and the wave function
sections.summary: In QM what we observe (discrete outcomes, e.g. an electron found at one place) is not what the theory says exists (a wave function spread over possibilities). Outcomes are predicted only probabilistically: each possible result has a complex amplitude, and its probability is the amplitude squared — the Born rule.

sections.title: Textbook rules: collapse and Copenhagen
sections.summary: Side-by-side recipes. Classical: set up the state, evolve with Newton's laws. Quantum textbook: evolve the wave function with the Schrödinger equation, but when measured it collapses to one outcome with Born-rule probability. Calling this 'the Copenhagen interpretation' hides that no one agrees on what measurement or an observer is. Footnote on squaring complex numbers (modulus squared).

chapters.title: 2. The Courageous Formulation: Austere Quantum Mechanics
chapters.summary: Introduces Many-Worlds as 'austere quantum mechanics' (AQM): keep only the wave function and the Schrödinger equation, drop the collapse postulate, and see what follows. The many worlds are not added; they were in the formalism all along.

sections.title: Shut up and calculate; Solvay 1927 and the Bohr–Einstein debates
sections.summary: Mermin's slogan for textbook attitudes. The 1927 Solvay Conference begins Einstein–Bohr exchanges. Key distinction: epistemic (wave function as knowledge, like a probability distribution in statistical mechanics) versus ontic (wave function as reality). Einstein lost in the popular telling, but his complaint — QM is incomplete — was about realism, not determinism.

sections.title: Austere QM: the wave function is reality
sections.summary: Two commitments: the wave function directly represents reality, and it always obeys the Schrödinger equation. A system's state is a superposition of every possible measurement outcome; 'where is the electron really?' has no answer beyond the wave function.

sections.title: The quantum/classical divide and the observer in superposition
sections.summary: If atoms are quantum, cameras and people made of atoms should be too. Treat measurement as an ordinary physical interaction: the camera ends up in a superposition correlated with the electron (entangled with it). Replace 'camera' with 'you' and the observer too is in a superposition of having seen each result.

sections.title: Everett’s move: worlds from the formalism
sections.summary: Hugh Everett (1957): stop resisting; each component of the entangled superposition is a separate world, each containing an observer who sees a definite outcome. Nothing is added to QM — hence the 'courageous' formulation.

sections.title: Open questions and the alternatives
sections.summary: Issues the book must face: when and why does the wave function split, why probabilities follow the Born rule, and whether the theory is 'empirically adequate'. The alternatives preview: add collapse, add hidden variables, or treat the wave function epistemically. Footnote on the Matthew Effect in quote attribution.

chapters.title: 3. Why Would Anybody Think This? How Quantum Mechanics Came to Be
chapters.summary: A semi-historical account of how the classical picture of particles plus fields broke down between 1900 and 1927, and how particles and fields were unified into a single wave function.

sections.title: Atoms and electrons
sections.summary: From Democritus to Dalton's chemical atoms (1803), Thomson's electron and Rutherford's nucleus. Nuclei provide mass; electrons in orbit account for all of chemistry.

sections.title: Fields and the late-19th-century picture
sections.summary: Nineteenth-century physics needed fields as well as particles: Maxwell's electromagnetic field, with light as an electromagnetic wave produced by shaken charges. By 1900 a complete theory seemed close.

sections.title: Planck and Einstein: quanta of light
sections.summary: Planck's constant (energy proportional to frequency) and Planck units from h, G and c. Einstein's 1905 proposal that light itself comes in particle-like quanta (photons), explaining the photoelectric effect despite Maxwell's waves.

sections.title: Atomic stability and Bohr’s orbits
sections.summary: A classical orbiting electron should radiate and spiral into the nucleus in a tiny fraction of a second (like planets emitting gravitational waves). Bohr's 1913 model allows only certain orbits; jumps between them emit light at definite frequencies, matching spectral lines. The 'old quantum theory' worked but no one was happy.

sections.title: Matrix mechanics and the Copenhagen circle
sections.summary: Heisenberg, Born, Jordan and Pauli build matrix mechanics around observable quantities only. The Copenhagen school's views were never uniform; note on Heisenberg's wartime role and on the lack of Nobel prizes for foundations.

sections.title: Matter waves and Schrödinger’s wave function
sections.summary: De Broglie (1924) gives electrons a wave; Schrödinger (1926) writes the equation for the 'wave function'. 'Quantum' does not mean pixelated: discreteness arises like the discrete notes of a vibrating string. Schrödinger's wave mechanics was received warmly; the Copenhagen youngsters were less gracious.

sections.title: The Hamiltonian, the Schrödinger equation and Born’s probabilities
sections.summary: The Schrödinger equation: the rate of change of the wave function is set by the Hamiltonian (energy) acting on it; know the Hamiltonian and you know the dynamics. Free wave functions spread out and do not look like particles, so Born proposed that their squared amplitude gives probabilities of finding a particle. Chapter recap.

chapters.title: 4. What Cannot Be Known, Because It Does Not Exist: Uncertainty and Complementarity
chapters.summary: Recasts the uncertainty principle as a fact about what wave functions are, not about clumsy measurements, then builds the mathematical picture used for the rest of the book: spins, qubits, and wave functions as vectors in Hilbert space.

sections.title: The uncertainty principle
sections.summary: Position and momentum are not properties an electron has but things we can observe. A wave function sharply peaked in position is a mixture of many wavelengths (momenta), and one with a single wavelength is spread over all space — so no state has both definite. This is not ignorance of a hidden truth.

sections.title: Quantum logic, briefly
sections.summary: Birkhoff and von Neumann's quantum logic rejects the distributive law for propositions about quantum systems; Carroll thinks classical logic is fine when applied correctly and the oddity lies in states, not logic.

sections.title: The double-slit experiment
sections.summary: Pellets through slits give two bands; water waves give an interference pattern. Electrons arrive one by one as dots yet build up an interference pattern — unless detectors at the slits record which way they went, which destroys the interference. Ignorance cannot cause interference, so the wave function is real.

sections.title: Spin and Stern–Gerlach magnets
sections.summary: Spin is quantized: along any chosen axis an electron is found spin-up or spin-down (right-hand rule picture). Sequential Stern–Gerlach magnets show that a vertically spin-up electron, measured horizontally, splits fifty-fifty — spin along different axes cannot all be definite.

sections.title: Qubits and wave functions as vectors
sections.summary: A qubit's state is a·(up) + b·(down) with complex amplitudes. Treat states as vectors: up and down are perpendicular basis vectors of a two-dimensional Hilbert space, and every state has length one. By Pythagoras the squared components sum to one, which is why probabilities are amplitudes squared.

sections.title: Complementarity as rotated bases
sections.summary: Different observables correspond to different sets of axes in Hilbert space; the up/down and right/left bases are rotated 45° relative to each other. A state aligned with one basis is a superposition in the other — the geometric origin of the uncertainty principle and Bohr's complementarity.

chapters.title: 5. Entangled Up in Blue: Wave Functions of Many Parts
chapters.summary: There is one wave function for the whole system, not one per particle. This chapter defines entanglement, walks through EPR and Bell's theorem, and shows that quantum mechanics is nonlocal in a precise sense while still forbidding faster-than-light signals.

sections.title: Scattering electrons and the wave function of many particles
sections.summary: Two electrons that collide have correlated outcomes because momentum is conserved: observing one tells you about the other. A multi-particle wave function assigns an amplitude to every configuration of all particles at once (configuration space) — ultimately one wave function of the universe for ~10^88 particles.

sections.title: Two qubits: product states and entangled states
sections.summary: Alice and Bob each hold one qubit. A state with both spin-up is unentangled; a superposition of (up,up) and (down,down) is entangled: Alice's result fixes Bob's. In textbook language her measurement collapses the shared state; in Many-Worlds it branches.

sections.title: No signaling
sections.summary: Entanglement seems to conflict with relativity, but Alice cannot choose her outcome, so Bob sees random results until they compare notes classically. No information travels faster than light.

sections.title: The EPR argument
sections.summary: Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen (1935) assume locality and 'elements of reality': since Alice can predict Bob's result in either basis without disturbing it, both values must exist beforehand, so QM is incomplete. Bohr's quick reply was widely thought to have settled it, though its content is unclear. Public reaction and Einstein's dislike of the paper's framing.

sections.title: Bell’s theorem and its tests
sections.summary: John Bell (1964): any local hidden-variable theory obeys an inequality on correlations measured along different axes; QM predicts violations. Experiments since the 1970s confirm QM. Loopholes include superdeterminism (our measurement choices are correlated in advance), tested by choosing settings with light from distant stars. Many-Worlds evades Bell because outcomes are not single.

chapters.title: Part Two · 6. Splitting the Universe: Decoherence and Parallel Worlds
chapters.summary: The core chapter on Many-Worlds: how Everett arrived at it at Princeton, how measurement becomes entanglement, and how decoherence explains why branches stop interfering and look like separate classical worlds.

sections.title: After EPR: Wheeler, Princeton and quantum gravity
sections.summary: Foundations went quiet after 1935 and were seen as an old man's hobby. John Wheeler at Princeton — 'radically conservative' — pushes into quantum gravity, where there is no outside observer to collapse the wave function of the universe.

sections.title: Everett and the wave function of the universe
sections.summary: Hugh Everett III, Wheeler's student, asks how to apply QM to a self-contained universe with no external measurer, and concludes the measurement rules must follow from the Schrödinger equation alone.

sections.title: Measurement as entanglement
sections.summary: Write the apparatus as a quantum system with ready/up/down states. Linearity of the Schrödinger equation turns spin superposition plus ready apparatus into an entangled superposition of (up, saw-up) and (down, saw-down). Alternatives all contort to avoid accepting this as the full description.

sections.title: Decoherence
sections.summary: H. Dieter Zeh (1970): the apparatus inevitably entangles with its environment (air molecules, photons). Once that happens the branches can no longer interfere — decoherence — explaining why wave functions seem to collapse and when branching happens.

sections.title: What counts as a world
sections.summary: A world is a branch of the wave function that has decohered and evolves independently of the others. A measurement is any interaction that entangles a system with the environment; an observer can be an earthworm, a microscope or a rock — consciousness plays no role.

sections.title: Everett’s thesis and its reception
sections.summary: Everett's 'amoeba with a life tree' draft; Wheeler's pressure to tone it down to placate Bohr; the Copenhagen rejection; Everett leaves physics for defense work. Bryce DeWitt revives the idea and a 1973 collection gives it the name 'Many-Worlds Interpretation'; Deutsch and others carry it on.

chapters.title: 7. Order and Randomness: Where Probability Comes From
chapters.summary: If Many-Worlds is deterministic and every outcome happens, what do probabilities mean, and why do they follow the Born rule? Carroll answers with self-locating uncertainty and derives the Born rule from a symmetry principle.

sections.title: The problem of probability in Many-Worlds
sections.summary: Wittgenstein's joke about how the Earth would look if the sun went round it. In a single-world theory probability is just frequency or credence about one outcome; in Many-Worlds both outcomes occur, raising the 'incoherence problem' (what is the probability of?) and the 'quantitative problem' (why amplitude squared?). The book's 'random number' thought experiment spawning many textual variants.

sections.title: What probability means: frequency vs credence
sections.summary: Frequentist probability (long-run fractions) versus Bayesian credence (degrees of belief, e.g. a team winning a championship). Many-Worlds needs the credence notion.

sections.title: Personal identity across branches
sections.summary: Before and after branching, who is 'you'? Following Derek Parfit, identity is psychological continuity (Relation R); in Many-Worlds one person becomes several future people, each continuous with the past one.

sections.title: Self-locating uncertainty
sections.summary: Decoherence is extremely fast, so there is a moment after branching when observers on each branch exist but do not yet know which branch they are on. Probability is uncertainty about one's own location in the wave function.

sections.title: Deriving the Born rule: branch counting and epistemic separability
sections.summary: Arbitrary measures (Albert's 'fatness measure') and naive branch counting fail; counting is inconsistent because extra measurements change the count. Instead require that credences not depend on what happens in distant parts of the universe (Epistemic Separability Principle). Splitting unequal branches into equal-amplitude pieces then forces probabilities equal to amplitude squared.

sections.title: Decision theory and other derivations
sections.summary: Deutsch and Wallace derive the Born rule from axioms of rational decision-making: a rational agent in a branching universe must weight outcomes by amplitude squared. Zurek's envariance offers another route. Showing we must act 'as if' probabilities hold is enough.

chapters.title: 8. Does This Ontological Commitment Make Me Look Fat? A Socratic Dialogue on Quantum Puzzles
chapters.summary: A dialogue in which Alice, a physicist, answers her skeptical father's objections to Many-Worlds over drinks. The chapter is a catalog of standard objections and replies.

sections.title: Extravagance and ontology
sections.summary: Isn't positing countless worlds extravagant? Reply: the theory's postulates are minimal; the worlds come automatically. Hilbert space is the same size in every version of QM. The real difficulty is the reverse: the formalism is so lean that mapping it onto experience takes work.

sections.title: Falsifiability and testability
sections.summary: Popper's criterion: Many-Worlds is falsifiable through its postulates (e.g., find a collapse). Unobservable consequences, like galaxies beyond our horizon, are accepted when a well-tested theory predicts them.

sections.title: Entropy, branching and the arrow of time
sections.summary: Why does branching only go toward the future? Because the early universe had low entropy (Boltzmann), and branching tracks increasing entanglement entropy; von Neumann's quantum entropy mirrors classical ignorance entropy.

sections.title: How many worlds are there?
sections.summary: Branches are emergent, coarse-grained descriptions, not fundamental, so their number is not sharply defined (Wallace's analogy to counting experiences). Hilbert space may be infinite-dimensional, or very large but finite; even a generous overestimate of branchings fits.

sections.title: Does everything happen?
sections.summary: No: only what the Schrödinger equation produces, with weights. Branches with absurd histories (fifty spin-ups in a row) exist but with tiny weight.

sections.title: Branching is local and relativity-friendly
sections.summary: Branching spreads outward from the interaction at or below light speed rather than happening simultaneously everywhere, so it does not conflict with special relativity; distant observers cannot tell whether they have 'branched yet'.

sections.title: Conservation of energy
sections.summary: Where does the energy for new worlds come from? Energy is computed from the whole wave function; each branch's energy counts weighted by its squared amplitude, so the total is conserved.

sections.title: Does she believe it?
sections.summary: Alice's honest credence: Many-Worlds is the best current bet; what matters is caring about the question.

chapters.title: 9. Other Ways: Alternatives to Many-Worlds
chapters.summary: A fair tour of the main rivals, each of which modifies, supplements or reinterprets the wave function to avoid many worlds, and of what each costs.

sections.title: The sociology of foundations
sections.summary: David Albert's graduate-school experience, David Bohm's exile and Everett's exit from physics illustrate how foundations work was discouraged. Many-Worlds' virtue is the simplicity of its postulates; all else is commentary.

sections.title: Modifying the Schrödinger equation
sections.summary: Schrödinger hoped his equation would describe everything. Steven Weinberg's nonlinear modification preserves total probability, but its simplest form allows faster-than-light signaling between entangled particles; patches exist but the idea has not caught on.

sections.title: Dynamical collapse: GRW and Penrose
sections.summary: GRW theory (Ghirardi, Rimini, Weber): each particle's wave function spontaneously localizes at a tiny random rate, but collapses cascade in macroscopic objects. Issues: collapse tails, a parameter-laden rule tied to particles rather than fields, possible energy non-conservation; testable via low-temperature experiments. Penrose's gravity-induced collapse. These amount to Everett plus a branch-pruning process.

sections.title: Hidden variables: von Neumann’s ‘proof’ and Bohm’s revival
sections.summary: Add variables (e.g., particle positions) beyond the wave function. Von Neumann's no-go proof assumed too much, as Grete Hermann pointed out and Bell later emphasized. Bohm (1952), after political troubles drove him abroad, revived de Broglie's pilot wave.

sections.title: Bohmian mechanics at work
sections.summary: Particles with definite positions are guided by the wave function; in the double-slit experiment each particle goes through one slit while the wave goes through both. Starting particles in a Born-rule distribution keeps it so ('quantum equilibrium'). Guidance is explicitly nonlocal and fits uneasily with relativity and with field theory; critics call it 'Many-Worlds in denial'.

sections.title: Epistemic approaches: QBism
sections.summary: Treat the wave function as an agent's personal degrees of belief. QBism (Fuchs, Schack, Caves, Mermin) uses Bayesian updating; measurement just updates beliefs. It offers insights into quantum information, but leaves open what reality is.

sections.title: Choosing among approaches
sections.summary: The tradeoff between underlying simplicity (Everett) and closeness to observed phenomena (others). Personal style decides weighting; Wallace's verdict that Everett is the only interpretive strategy that fits physics as practiced, especially quantum field theory.

chapters.title: 10. The Human Side: Living and Thinking in a Quantum Universe
chapters.summary: What, if anything, Many-Worlds changes about decisions, ethics, free will and consciousness. Mostly: very little, once branch weights are taken into account.

sections.title: Quantum decision-making
sections.summary: The 'Universe Splitter' app uses a quantum measurement to choose between options, creating worlds in which each choice is made; this does not increase anything worth having.

sections.title: Quantum suicide and immortality
sections.summary: If a device kills you on one branch, some version always survives. Carroll's reply: you are allowed to care about branches you won't experience, so quantum Russian roulette is as bad as it seems; don't take bets that lose on branch weight.

sections.title: Ethics across branches
sections.summary: Should we value total or weighted utility across branches? Weight each branch by its Born-rule measure (as with energy); deontological ethics is largely unaffected. A tongue-in-cheek 'QUMaD' rule shows why naive branch counting leads to absurdities.

sections.title: Agents and decisions as emergent and classical
sections.summary: People can be described as particles obeying the Schrödinger equation or as agents with choices; both descriptions are valid at their own level. Decisions in brains are classical processes; branching does not create choices.

sections.title: Free will
sections.summary: Free will versus determinism is the wrong pairing; determinism is opposed to indeterminism. Many-Worlds is deterministic yet not predictable for those inside it. Compatibilism: free will is real as an emergent, useful concept like tables and temperature.

sections.title: Consciousness and the measurement problem
sections.summary: Rejects the idea that consciousness collapses the wave function. Physicalism: consciousness arises from brains, which are ordinary physical systems. Wigner's consciousness-causes-collapse, dualism, idealism and panpsychism are considered and found unnecessary; reality exists independently of observers.

chapters.title: Part Three · 11. Why Is There Space? Emergence and Locality
chapters.summary: Begins the program of finding space and gravity inside quantum mechanics rather than quantizing classical gravity. Introduces emergence, explains why the world looks classical in some bases and not others, and identifies locality of interactions as the key.

sections.title: Gravity resists quantization: start from the quantum
sections.summary: Other forces are fine as quantized classical field theories; gravity is not. Rather than quantize general relativity, start with an abstract wave function and Schrödinger equation and ask how spacetime could emerge — the Many-Worlds approach needs no added superstructure.

sections.title: Locality
sections.summary: Locality — things interact only with nearby things and nothing travels faster than light — is a defining feature of space in relativistic physics.

sections.title: Emergent worlds and effective descriptions
sections.summary: Worlds are emergent: a higher-level description that throws away information yet remains predictive. Branches are carved from the wave function in the right way when each obeys approximately classical laws, e.g. Newtonian gravity for rocket flights. Emergence is special, not automatic.

sections.title: Why position, not momentum?
sections.summary: In Hamiltonian mechanics position and momentum are symmetric, and configuration space is huge, yet we live in three-dimensional space. The symmetry is broken by dynamical locality: interactions depend on positions.

sections.title: Schrödinger’s cat and the preferred basis
sections.summary: A cat and a sleeping-gas version of the thought experiment. Why do branches look like 'awake' or 'asleep' rather than superpositions of them? Because those states are localized in space, and interactions with the environment are local — decoherence picks the pointer basis.

chapters.title: 12. A World of Vibrations: Quantum Field Theory
chapters.summary: Quantum field theory as the wave function of field configurations. Particles are excitations of fields, empty space has rich structure, and the vacuum is highly entangled — the raw material for emergent geometry.

sections.title: Action at a distance and the rise of fields
sections.summary: Newton's discomfort with gravity acting instantly at a distance; fields fix it. The 'Core Theory' (Standard Model plus gravity) is built from fields; quantizing a classical field theory in preexisting space is the usual route.

sections.title: From particle wave functions to field wave functions
sections.summary: For many particles there is one wave function on configuration space. In QFT, the wave function assigns amplitudes to every configuration of the field: waviness on top of waviness.

sections.title: Modes, the vacuum and particles
sections.summary: Decompose a field into vibrational modes with quantized energies; the state with every mode at lowest energy is the vacuum. One quantum of excitation looks like a particle. Electrons, quarks and photons are vibrations of their fields.

sections.title: Vacuum energy and the cosmological constant
sections.summary: Empty space has energy, measured as the accelerating expansion of the universe. Adding zero-point energies up to a Planck-scale cutoff gives an answer ~10^122 too big — the cosmological constant problem.

sections.title: ‘Quantum fluctuations’ and whether particles are really there
sections.summary: Nothing in the vacuum fluctuates; the term describes the spread of possible measurement outcomes in a stationary state. Particle number depends on how and where one observes — particles are what the theory looks like under particular kinds of observation.

sections.title: The entangled vacuum
sections.summary: Divide space into regions: the vacuum is entangled across every boundary, and unentangling them would cost infinite energy. Each region's Hilbert space is infinite-dimensional in QFT. The Reeh–Schlieder theorem: poking a local region can, in principle, produce any state.

chapters.title: 13. Breathing in Empty Space: Finding Gravity within Quantum Mechanics
chapters.summary: Carroll's own research program: start from a vector in Hilbert space and a Hamiltonian, find locality and a way to split into subsystems, use entanglement between pieces to define distances, and recover something like Einstein's equation. Time is handled through clocks inside the universe.

sections.title: Where QFT ends
sections.summary: QFT accounts for every experiment, but gravity is missing. The goal: understand when branches of the wave function look like quantum fields propagating in a curved spacetime.

sections.title: General relativity in brief
sections.summary: Spacetime unifies space and time; observers divide it differently. Einstein's equation relates curvature to energy and momentum (Wheeler: matter tells spacetime how to curve, spacetime tells matter how to move). There is no preferred way to identify points across different geometries (sphere vs torus), complicating quantization.

sections.title: Why quantum gravity is hard
sections.summary: Gravity is ~10^43 times weaker than electric repulsion, so data are scarce. Effective field theory of gravity works at low energies. Main approaches: string theory and loop quantum gravity; conceptual problems may not be fixed by technical progress.

sections.title: Entropy and entanglement entropy
sections.summary: Boltzmann entropy counts arrangements; entanglement entropy measures how much a subsystem is entangled with the rest. In Many-Worlds an observer's branch can look like a mixed state.

sections.title: Jacobson: Einstein’s equation from entanglement
sections.summary: Ted Jacobson (1995): assuming entropy proportional to the area bounding a region and applying thermodynamics, Einstein's equation follows. Changing a region's entanglement changes its geometry.

sections.title: Finding subsystems and locality inside Hilbert space
sections.summary: With only a state and a Hamiltonian, which way of factoring Hilbert space into subsystems is right? The one in which interactions are local: each degree of freedom interacts with a few others, forming a network that is the skeleton of space.

sections.title: Distance from entanglement: emergent geometry
sections.summary: Define distance by mutual information: strongly entangled degrees of freedom are close, weakly entangled ones far. Carroll's 2016 and 2018 papers with Cao and Michalakis: geometry emerges and, under perturbation, curves in a way consistent with Jacobson's reasoning — a promising but partial result.

sections.title: The problem of time
sections.summary: Maybe time also emerges. The Wheeler–DeWitt equation says the universe's total state does not evolve. Page and Wootters: entangle a clock subsystem with the rest; conditioned on clock readings, the rest appears to evolve. Time as 'what the clock reads in this part of the wave function'. Nods to ER=EPR.

chapters.title: 14. Beyond Space and Time: Holography, Black Holes, and the Limits of Locality
chapters.summary: Black holes show that the simple 'nearest-neighbor' picture of emergent space is incomplete: gravity is holographic, and its degrees of freedom are not localized in space.

sections.title: Hawking radiation
sections.summary: Hawking (1974) applied QFT in curved spacetime: black holes emit thermal radiation, small ones are hotter, and they slowly evaporate. Temperature formula on his gravestone.

sections.title: The information-loss puzzle
sections.summary: If radiation is purely thermal, information about what fell in is lost, violating unitarity. Most physicists think information escapes, and expect the explanation to reveal quantum gravity.

sections.title: Bekenstein entropy: area, not volume
sections.summary: Bekenstein (another Wheeler student) argued black holes have entropy proportional to horizon area. Unlike QFT entanglement entropy it is finite. Black holes are the maximum-entropy objects in a region, implying a finite number of degrees of freedom — including for our cosmological horizon.

sections.title: The holographic principle and the black hole interior
sections.summary: Physics of a three-dimensional region may be encoded on its two-dimensional boundary ('t Hooft, Susskind). Whether the interior of a black hole exists independently becomes subtle.
terms: degrees of freedom on the boundary

sections.title: AdS/CFT
sections.summary: Maldacena (1997): gravity in anti–de Sitter space is equivalent to a conformal field theory without gravity on its boundary. Ryu–Takayanagi and Van Raamsdonk link boundary entanglement to bulk geometry. But our universe has positive vacuum energy — AdS/CFT is the brightest streetlight, not necessarily where the keys are.

sections.title: Horizon complementarity and firewalls
sections.summary: Infalling and distant observers tell different but consistent stories (black hole complementarity); the firewall argument challenges this. Lesson: locality is emergent and breaks down near horizons; Many-Worlds may help, though many quantum-gravity researchers don't yet think so.

chapters.title: Epilogue: Everything Is Quantum
chapters.summary: What Einstein might have thought of Many-Worlds: repelled, but drawn to its realism and determinism. The book's title comes from Einstein's childhood compass and his conviction that something deeply hidden lies behind things. Quantum technology (computing, cryptography, information) is pushing physicists to take foundations seriously; the classical world is an approximation and everything is quantum.

chapters.title: Appendix: The Story of Virtual Particles
chapters.summary: The particle-centred view of QFT that working physicists use, explained in contrast to the book's vacuum-centred treatment: Feynman diagrams, virtual particles, loops, renormalization and effective field theory.

sections.title: Feynman diagrams as stories
sections.summary: When fields are weakly interacting we can describe processes in particle language; Feynman diagrams (e.g., electron and positron annihilating into a photon) are bookkeeping for calculations, not literal histories.

sections.title: Virtual particles
sections.summary: Internal lines represent 'virtual particles' that need not obey normal energy-mass relations; really they are field modes, not particles popping in and out of existence.

sections.title: Loops and infinities
sections.summary: Closed loops let virtual particles carry any momentum, so naive sums diverge. Even an isolated particle is dressed by a cloud of virtual particles, shifting its measured mass and charge.

sections.title: Renormalization and effective field theory
sections.summary: Kenneth Wilson (1970s): divergences come from high energies; impose a cutoff and the low-energy physics becomes insensitive to what happens beyond it. Effective field theory explains why physics is predictive and why high-energy physics is hard to probe.

title: Something Deeply Hidden: Quantum Worlds and the Emergence of Spacetime
note: A popular-science book treated here as a textbook. The book has fourteen chapters in three parts (Spooky, Splitting, Spacetime) plus prologue, epilogue and an appendix; its chapters have unnamed section breaks only, so the sections below are our own topical divisions, with page ranges in the PDF (this ebook carries no printed page numbers). Further reading, references and index are not broken out. See also the [review page](https://vwulf.github.io/ettuge/Books/influential/something-deeply-hidden). Summaries are in our own words; the text stays in the PDF.
summary: Sean Carroll argues that quantum mechanics is not inherently mysterious; physicists have simply refused to ask what it describes. Part One builds the essentials — wave functions, the Born rule, uncertainty as geometry of vectors in Hilbert space, spin, entanglement, EPR and Bell — and introduces 'austere' quantum mechanics: the wave function plus the Schrödinger equation and nothing else. Part Two shows how decoherence turns that single wave function into effectively separate, branching classical worlds (Everett's Many-Worlds), how probability and the Born rule arise from self-locating uncertainty, answers standard objections in a dialogue, compares the rivals (GRW collapse, Bohmian mechanics, QBism), and draws out consequences for ethics, free will and consciousness. Part Three turns to quantum field theory and gravity: rather than quantizing general relativity, start from an abstract quantum state and recover space from entanglement (distance from mutual information, Einstein's equation à la Jacobson), time from internal clocks, and confront holography, black-hole entropy and AdS/CFT. An appendix explains virtual particles and renormalization.
